source_text: Σὸν δέ ἐστι κτῆμα ἡ ἡτοιμασμένη βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν. Ὅρια πατέρων μὴ κινήσῃς. Μὴ ἐπιθυμήσῃς τῆς τοῦ πλησίον χώρας. Μὴ, αὔλακα αὔλακι προστιθεὶς, κατὰ μικρὸν αὔξανε τὴν σήν. Ὅσον γὰρ πλατύνεις ἐκ τῆς ἀλλοτρίας προσθήκης τὴν γῆν, τοσούτῳ μακροτέραν σοι τὴν ἁμαρτίαν κατασκευάζεις. Καὶ ἡ μὲν γῆ ἐνταῦθα παραμένει, κατὰ μικρόν σοι προσχωρηθεῖσα, καὶ διὰ τῆς πλεονεξίας γενομένη, οὐκέτι σή, ἀλλὰ τῶν μετὰ σὲ, καὶ ἀφίης ἄδικον τῷ διαδεχομένῳ τὸν βίον· «Ἡ γῆ ἕστηκεν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα,» ἡ δὲ ἁμαρτία ἀκολουθήσει σοι, ὡς σκιὰ παρεπομένη τῇ ψυχῇ. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ σκιὰ τῷ σώματι ἕπεται, οὕτω καὶ ἡ ἁμαρτία τῇ ψυχῇ συμπέφυκε. Μὴ ἴσθι σεαυτῷ πληθύνων τὴν ἁμαρ τίαν. Οὐδαμοῦ γὰρ ἵσταται τῆς πλεονεξίας ἡ νόσος, ἀλλ' ὁμοία ἐστὶ τῇ τοῦ πυρὸς φύσει. Καὶ γὰρ τὸ πῦρ ἐπειδὰν καταπρήσεως ἅψηται, σπεύδει πᾶσαν ἐπινεμηθῆναι τὴν ὕλην, καὶ οὐδεὶς αὐτὸ στῆσαι δύ ναται, πρὶν ἂν ἐπιλείπῃ ἡ ὕλη. Τὸν δὲ πλεονέ κτην τί δύναται ἐπισχεῖν; Πυρός ἐστι χαλεπώτερος, πάντα διὰ συνεχείας νεμόμενος. Ἔλαβε τὰ τοῦ πλησίον· ἄλλος ἀνεφάνη γείτων· καὶ τὰ ἐκείνου ἐξιδιοποιήσατο. Οὐ τοῖς κατόπιν προσέξει, ὅτι πολ λά· ἀλλὰ τοῖς λείπουσιν, ὅτι γείτονας κέκτηται. Οὐκ εὐφραίνει τὰ κτηθέντα, ἀλλὰ λυπεῖ τὰ λειπόμενα· οὐ τῇ ἀπολαύσει τῶν συναχθέντων προσέχει, ἀλλ' ἑαυτὸν ἐκδαπανᾷ τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ τῆς τοῦ πλείο νος κτήσεως. Εἶτα ἀγρυπνίαι ἐντεῦθεν, αἱ μέριμναι, αἱ φροντίδες. Ὅσον αὔξει ὁ πλοῦτος, τοσοῦ τον φέρει τοῦ βίου τὸ μεριμνητικόν. Δικαστὴς προσδοκᾶται, καὶ ὁ πλεονέκτης περισκοπεῖ μὴ εἰς δικαστήρια παρασυρῇ· μὴ ὀρφανὸς τὸ δάκρυον ἑαυ τοῦ ἐπὶ δικαστηρίου δημοσιεύσῃ. Βουλεύεται ἐν νυκτὶ, τίνας τῶν πικρῶν συνηγόρων παρασκευάσει, ἵνα ψευδεῖς μαρτυρίας ἐκμισθώσηται· πῶς ἐκπο λιορκήσει τὸν ἐν τῇ ἐρημίᾳ, καταδυναστεύσει δὲ τούτου, καὶ ἐν δικαστηρίῳ τὴν ἀλήθειαν κλέψας· ἀμφοτέρους δὲ ἀναλώσει, καὶ τὸν δικαστὴν παρακρουσάμενος, καὶ τὸν νήπιον πλεονεκτήσας. Αὗται αἱ μέριμναι δαπανῶσι τοῦ πλεονέκτου τὴν ψυ χήν. Κύων ὑλακτεῖ, καὶ ὁ πλούσιος νομίζει κλέπτην εἶναι. Μυὸς ψόφος, καὶ τοῦ πλουσίου ἡ καρδία πηδᾷ· τὸν παῖδα ὑποπτεύει, πάντα δι' ὑποψίας ἔχει· υἱοὺς αὐξανομένους ὥσπερ ἐπιβούλους ὁρᾷ, ὅτι ἡ ἡλικία αὐτῶν τὴν διαδοχὴν κατεπείγει. Τοῖς πλεονέκταις καὶ ἑτέρα ἐστὶ νόσος. Τὸν βίον αὐ τοῦ ἐπὶ δακτύλων τίθησι· τὸν μὲν δημοσιεύει, τὸν δὲ κατορωρυγμένον ἔχει πρὸς ἐλπίδας τὰς ἀδήλους ἀποτιθέμενος· ἐλπίδας τὰς οὐκ ἐλπίδας. Εἰ γὰρ πρὸς ἐλπίδας ἦν ἡ ἀπόθεσις, πρὸς τὴν αἰωνίαν ἐλπίδα ἐγένετο ἂν ἡ παρασκευή. Νῦν δὲ ὑποκρύπτει τῇ κλίνῃ τὸν πλοῦτον τὸν ἄδηλον, τὴν ἐπερχομένην ζημίαν ἀποστρέφειν οἰόμενος. Ἀλλ' εἰ μὲν ἥξει ποτὲ ἡ χρεία, ἄδηλον· ἥξει μέντοι καιρὸς, ἐν ᾧ μεταμεληθήσῃ, μὴ οἰκονομήσας τὸν πλοῦτον. Τοῦτο πρόδηλον, κἀγώ εἰμι ὁ ἐγγυώμενος . Ἀνάγκη μὲν γὰρ περὶ πάντων τῶν παθῶν διαλέγεσθαι, ὑπομιμνήσκοντα ὑμᾶς· ὑμᾶς δὲ προσέχοντας λαμβάνειν τὴν ἐκ τῶν λόγων ὠφέλειαν, ἵνα, ἀποδυσά μενος ἕκαστος, ὥσπερ γῆρας ὄφεως, τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, οὕτως ἐπανέλθοι γεγυμνωμένος, καὶ ἔχων τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτῷ ἐπανθοῦσαν, ἕτερος ἐξ ἑτέρου γενόμενος.
thought_title: Greed widens sin and wears out the greedy man
orientation: The preacher continues his treatment of greed as a destructive passion that needs its own Scriptural cure.
pass_a_gloss: But your possession is the prepared kingdom of the heavens. Do not move the boundaries of the fathers. Do not desire the land of the neighbor. Do not, adding furrow to furrow, increase your own little by little. For by as much as you widen the earth from the addition of what belongs to another, by so much longer a sin you prepare for yourself. And the earth remains here, having come over to you little by little, and having become through greed no longer yours but that of those after you, and you leave injustice to the one who succeeds to the livelihood; 'The earth stands forever,' but the sin will follow you, as a shadow attending the soul. For just as the shadow follows the body, so also the sin has grown together with the soul. Do not be one who multiplies the sin for yourself. For the sickness of greed stands nowhere, but it is like the nature of fire. For fire, whenever it lays hold of burning, hastens to feed upon all the material, and no one is able to stop it, before the material fails. But what is able to hold back the greedy man? He is harder than fire, feeding on all things through continuity. He took the things of the neighbor; another neighbor appeared; and he made that man's things his own. He does not attend to the things behind, because they are many; but to the things left, because they have neighbors. The things acquired do not gladden, but the things left behind grieve; he does not attend to the enjoyment of the things gathered together, but he spends himself with the desire for the acquisition of the more. Then from this come sleepless nights, the anxieties, the cares. By as much as wealth increases, by so much does it bring the anxiety of livelihood. A judge is expected, and the greedy man looks round lest he be dragged into courts; lest an orphan publish his own tear in court. He deliberates in the night, what bitter advocates he will prepare, in order that he may hire false testimonies; how he will besiege the man in the desert, and will overpower him, and having stolen the truth in court; and he will consume both, both having deceived the judge, and having gained advantage over the child. These anxieties consume the soul of the greedy man. A dog barks, and the rich man supposes it is a thief. A sound of a mouse, and the heart of the rich man leaps; he suspects the servant, he holds all things in suspicion; he sees growing sons as plotters, because their age hastens the succession. For greedy men there is also another sickness. He puts his livelihood on his fingers; the one part he publishes, but the buried part he keeps, laying it up for unclear hopes; hopes that are not hopes. For if the laying away were for hopes, the preparation would have come to be for the eternal hope. But now he hides the unseen wealth in his bed, supposing to turn away the coming loss. But whether the need will ever come is unclear; yet a time will come, in which you will repent, not having managed the wealth. This is manifest, and I am the one who guarantees it. For there is need to discuss all the passions, reminding you; and for you, attending, to receive the benefit from the words, in order that, each having stripped off the sin like old skin of a snake, so he may return back stripped, and having righteousness blossoming for him, having become another from another.

pass_b_english: Your true possession is the kingdom of heaven made ready for you. Do not move the boundaries set by your fathers. Do not covet your neighbor's land. Do not add furrow to furrow and enlarge your own field little by little. The wider you make your land by taking what belongs to another, the longer you make your own sin. The land stays here after you have drawn it to yourself little by little. What you gained by greed will no longer be yours. It will belong to those who come after you, and you will leave injustice behind for the one who inherits your life. Scripture says, “The earth stands forever” (Ecclesiastes 1:4). But your sin will follow you like a shadow that attends the soul.

A shadow follows the body, and in the same way sin clings to the soul. So do not keep multiplying sin against yourself. This sickness of greed never comes to a stop. It is like fire in its nature. When fire catches dry fuel, it rushes to spread through all the wood. No one can halt it until the wood runs out.

What can hold back the greedy man? He is harder to stop than fire, and he keeps consuming everything in his path. He seized his neighbor's land. Then another neighbor appeared, and he made that man's land his own. He pays no heed to what lies behind him, though it is much. He fixes his eyes on what remains, because his neighbors still hold it. What he has gained brings him no joy, and what is left grieves him. He takes no pleasure in what he has gathered. He wastes himself away with desire to gain still more. From this come sleepless nights, anxieties, and cares. The greater his wealth grows, the greater worry fills his life. He expects a judge, and the greedy man looks about in fear that he will be dragged into court. He fears that an orphan will lay his tears openly before the court. At night he plots which hard advocates he will engage and how he will hire false testimony. He plans how he will besiege the defenseless man, how he will crush him, and how he will steal the truth in court. In the end he destroys them both. He tricks the judge, and he cheats the child of his due. These are the cares that consume the soul of the greedy man.

A dog barks, and the rich man thinks a thief has come. A mouse stirs, and the rich man's heart leaps. He suspects his servant. He views everything with suspicion. He sees his growing sons as plotters against him, because their coming of age hastens his succession. Greedy men suffer from another sickness as well. A man counts his livelihood on his fingers. One part he declares openly, and the other part he keeps buried. He stores it away for an uncertain future, for hopes that are no hopes. If he were truly storing it for hope, he would be preparing for the hope that lasts forever. As it is, he hides his secret wealth beside his bed, and he thinks he will turn away the loss to come. Whether that need will ever come is uncertain. Yet a time will surely come when you will repent for failing to use your wealth well. That is clear, and I vouch for it. I must speak of all these passions to remind you, and you must listen and take the profit from these words. Let each of you strip off sin like a snake casts off its old skin. Then go home stripped bare, with righteousness blooming afresh upon you, changed from one man into another.
notes: Spaced breaks in ἁμαρ τίαν, δύ ναται, πλεονέ κτην, πολ λά, πλείo νος, ἑαυ τοῦ, ἐκπο λιορκήσει, ψυ χήν, αὐ τοῦ are line break artefacts, read as single words; no text invented.

problems.quote: In the end he destroys both sides.
problems.source_quote: ἀμφοτέρους δὲ ἀναλώσει, καὶ τὸν δικαστὴν παρακρουσάμενος, καὶ τὸν νήπιον πλεονεκτήσας
problems.why: He ruins both persons—the judge and the child—by deceiving the one and defrauding the other, not two opposing sides.
problems.fix: He ruins them both, misleading the judge and defrauding the child.
problems.ruling: ἀμφοτέρους ἀναλώσει, καὶ τὸν δικαστὴν παρακρουσάμενος, καὶ τὸν νήπιον πλεονεκτήσας: both are judge and child, not 'both sides'; misleads reader.

problems.quote: A man puts his livelihood on his fingers.
problems.source_quote: Τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ δακτύλων τίθησι
problems.why: The idiom means he reckons his property by counting on his fingers; the English sentence cannot be understood.
problems.fix: He counts his livelihood on his fingers.
problems.ruling: ἐπὶ δακτύλων τίθησι means he counts/reckons his livelihood on his fingers; 'puts his livelihood on his fingers' is unintelligible and loses the counting idiom.

problems.quote: Then go home unburdened, with righteousness blooming afresh upon you
problems.source_quote: οὕτως ἐπανέλθοι γεγυμνωμένος, καὶ ἔχων τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτῷ ἐπανθοῦσαν
problems.why: He returns stripped naked, like shed skin, with righteousness flowering on him; “unburdened” replaces that image.
problems.fix: Then return home stripped bare, with righteousness flowering upon you.
problems.ruling: γεγυμνωμένος, 'stripped', after ἀποδυσάμενος (strip off sin) means returning stripped of sin; 'unburdened' loses it, and 'go home' misses ἐπανέλθοι. Flowering ἐπανθοῦσαν is kept.
